name: Price per weight
seoTitle: Price per weight Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Price per weight: work out weight (Option A) from number of items and the cost. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply number of items, the cost and the price per weight and the Price per weight calculator solves for weight (Option A). That makes it useful for a practical question that turns up in daily life. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Price per weight calculator work?
sections.html:
The Price per weight calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports weight (Option A) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type); then you type in number of items (Option A), the cost (Option A), the price per weight (Option A) and the weight (Option B).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Price per weight calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Weight=cost ÷ (number of items × price per weight)
Cost=number of items × price per weight × weight
You save=the absolute value of (cost ÷ (number of items × weight) − cost ÷ (number of items × weight))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Type set to Weight, Number of items = 10, Cost = 10 and Price per weight = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Weight = 0.1 g.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Weight = 0.1 g should be roughly the size you expected from Type set to Weight and Number of items = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Price per weight calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — number of items, the cost and the price per weight — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Price per weight calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns weight (Option A), derived from number of items, the cost and the price per weight. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Price per weight calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for number of items, the cost and the price per weight, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter weight (Option A) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Weight (Option A) opens in grams and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Weight = 0.1 g. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Price per weight calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
